titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §178–184: priestesses and their inheritance (xxx 61 – xxxii 30)
part: Laws §178–184 · priestesses, dowries & inheritance (Col. xxx 61 – xxxii 30)
about: Seven laws on women who belong to a god and on what they inherit from their fathers. A priestess whose father gave her a dowry and wrote a tablet for her, but did not write that she may give her estate to whomever she pleases, holds her field and orchard for life, and her brothers inherit them; if her brothers fail to give her her rations of grain, oil and wool, she may let the land to a tenant, who must keep supporting her (§178). If the tablet does allow her to give her estate where she pleases, her brothers have no claim against her (§179). A woman of this kind whose father gave her no dowry takes a share in her father’s house like one heir (§180); a qadištum or a NU.PAR dedicated to a god without a dowry, one third of an heir’s share, for her lifetime (§181); and a “wife of Marduk” of Babylon without a dowry or tablet takes one third of an heir’s share outright, performs no fief-duty on it, and may give her estate wherever she pleases (§182). The last two laws concern the šugītum: if her father gave her a dowry and a husband she has no further share in his house (§183), but if he gave her neither, her brothers must give her a dowry in proportion to the means of the house and give her to a husband (§184). The classes of priestess are named by Sumerian sign-groups (NIN.AN, SAL, NU.GIG, NU.PAR, SAL.É.GI₄.A) and by words whose exact meaning is still argued; the notes mark each reading as certain or uncertain.

sentences.l: If a-priestess(?), a-SAL(?), or-else a-woman a-zikrum, whom her-father a-dowry has-given-her,
sentences.i: If a priestess (?), a SAL-woman (?), or a woman of the zikrum class, to whom her father has given a dowry,
sentences.n: The first of seven laws on women dedicated to a god, and a law with a long “if”, so read it clause by clause; this unit only names the woman. šumma is “if” as always, but the subject is a woman. NIN.AN is a Sumerogram of two signs, read ugbabtum “priestess” as at §127: UNCERTAIN (Harper gives no reading and later editions read the signs differently). The sign after it is Harper’s ŠAL(?), the woman-sign SAL with his own question mark; I give it as SAL and no more, since a lone SAL is read as a class of priestess by some later editions (compare §40), UNCERTAIN. ù lū zinništum zikrum is “or else a woman, a zikrum”: ù “and, or”, lū “or indeed”, SAL read zinništum “woman” (as at §141–152), and zi-ik-ru-um, zikrum, the name of a class of woman; it is not the zikrum “name” of the prologue, and what the class was I cannot say, UNCERTAIN. ša abūša šeriqtam išruqušim is “whom her father has given a dowry”: ša opens a relative clause that runs through the next unit (watch for this pattern; it comes back at every law); abūša is “her father”, šeriqtam “a dowry” (§138), and išruqušim is išruq, “he gave (as a gift)”, from šarāqum, with the subjunctive -u and -šim “to her” (short u before -šim, the house rule); the -šim looks back to the woman, so the clause reads “whom … he gave her a dowry”. Harper prints iš-ru-qu-ši-im; the sign is KU, read qu₂.

sentences.l: a-tablet he-has-written-for-her, in-the-tablet which he-wrote-for-her,
sentences.i: and has written a tablet for her, and in the tablet he wrote for her
sentences.n: The relative clause goes on: the father also wrote a tablet. ṭuppam išṭurušim is “a tablet he has written for her”: ṭuppam is DUB-pa-am, and išṭurušim is the same -u + -šim form as before, from šaṭārum “to write”. ina ṭuppim ša išṭurušim is “in the tablet which he wrote for her”: ṭuppim (DUB-pi-im) after ina, then a second ša-clause. The sentence stays open; what the tablet did not say comes next.

sentences.l: her-estate wherever it-is-pleasing to-her to-give not he-has-written-for-her-and, as-much-as her-heart not he-has-let-her-have,
sentences.i: has not written for her that she may give her estate to whomever it pleases her, and has not let her have as much as she wishes,
sentences.n: What the tablet left out: two things, both with lā “not”. warkassa ēma elīša ṭābu nadānam is “her estate, wherever it is pleasing to her, to give”: warkassa is warkatum “estate” + -ša “her” (t+š written ss, the spelling wa-ar-ka-za of §141–152), ēma “wherever”, elīša ṭābu “it is pleasing to her” (eli “upon”, ṭâbum “to be good”; the verb is in the subjunctive -u after ēma), and nadānam the infinitive “to give”; I read the clause as “to give her estate to whomever she pleases” (house rendering). lā išṭuršimma is “he has not written for her, and”: išṭur + -šim “to her” + -ma; lā with the preterite is “has not”. mala libbiša is “as much as her heart (wants)”. lā ušamziši is “he has not let her have”: a Š-stem preterite (the spelling u-ša-am-zi-ši) with -ši “her”; the verb behind it is UNCERTAIN, and the sense “let her have her fill” is taken from the context.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, her-field and her-orchard her-brothers shall-take-and,
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, her brothers shall take her field and her orchard, and
sentences.n: The “then” part of the law begins here. warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku is “after the father has gone to his fate” (as §170 and §165). eqlša is “her field”: A.ŠÀ, two Sumerogram signs (A and ŠÀ), then ša “her” spelled out; Harper prints eqil-ša. u kirâša is “and her orchard”: {giš}KIRI₆, the wood-sign silent and the SAR sign read KIRI₆ (kirûm, as in §26–41), again with ša. aḫḫūša is “her brothers”: aḫḫū, the nominative plural of aḫum “brother”, with ša. ileqqūma is “they shall take, and”: leqûm + the plural -ū + -ma, spelled i-li-qu₂-ma (the sign KU, read qu₂).

sentences.l: in-proportion-to the-strength of-her-share grain-ration oil-ration and wool-ration they-shall-give-her-and her-heart they-shall-make-good.
sentences.i: and they shall give her, in proportion to her share, the grain, oil and wool rations, and so content her.
sentences.n: What the brothers must give her. kīma emūq zittiša is “in proportion to the strength of her share”: kīma “like, in proportion to”, emūq “strength” (no ending, a construct), zittiša “her share” (zittum, as at §165). ŠE.BA, Ì.BA and SIG.BA are three Sumerograms of two signs each, which I leave unread: ŠE is “grain”, Ì (Harper’s NI) “oil”, SIG “wool”, each with BA “ration, allowance”, so “grain, oil and wool rations”; the Akkadian words behind them are UNCERTAIN (first time in this work; Harper writes NI.BA and ŠIG.BA). inaddinūšimma is “they shall give her, and”: inaddinū (present plural of nadānum) + -šim + -ma; Harper writes the -šim here with one sign, TAG, read šim (it is the sign of šum), where other lines spell ši-im with two. libbaša uṭabbū is “they shall make her heart good”: libbum “heart”, uṭabbū the present plural of the D-stem of ṭâbum, “they shall content her”.

sentences.l: If her-brothers in-proportion-to the-strength of-her-share grain-ration oil-ration and wool-ration not have-given-her-and her-heart not have-made-good,
sentences.i: If her brothers have not given her the grain, oil and wool rations in proportion to her share, and have not contented her,
sentences.n: A second šumma at once: the brothers fail. It is the previous unit’s wording turned negative and put in the perfect (watch the contrast, present against perfect): ittadnūšimma is the perfect of nadānum with the plural -ū, -šim “to her” and -ma, spelled it-ta-ad-nu-ši-im-ma, and uṭṭibbū is the perfect of the D-stem of ṭâbum, “they have contented (her)”, spelled uṭ-ṭi-ib-bu with the sign UD read uṭ. lā “not” stands before each. This is the protasis; the ruling is the next unit.

sentences.l: her-field and her-orchard to-a-tenant who to-her is-pleasing she-shall-give-and, her-tenant shall-keep-supporting-her.
sentences.i: she shall give her field and her orchard to a tenant who is pleasing to her, and her tenant shall keep supporting her.
sentences.n: The ruling: she lets the land out herself. eqlša u kirâša as above, now objects of inaddinma “she shall give, and”. ana irrišim ša elīša ṭābu is “to a tenant who is pleasing to her”: irrišum “tenant”, then the ša-clause with elīša ṭābu as at §178. irrissa is “her tenant”: irrišum + -ša, the š+š spelled with ZA (ir-ri-za; the same spelling as irrissu at §42–51). ittanaššiši is “he shall keep supporting her”: the iterative present (Gtn: it-ta-na-… “again and again”) of našûm “to carry, bear” + -ši “her”, spelled it-ta-na-aš-ši-ši, with the single-wedge sign AŠ read aš; “supporting” is my sense for what a tenant owes her, UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: the-field, the-orchard and whatever her-father has-given-her as-long-as she-lives she-shall-have-the-use-of; for silver not she-shall-give,
sentences.i: She shall have the use of the field, the orchard and whatever her father gave her as long as she lives; she shall not give (them) for silver,
sentences.n: What she may and may not do with the land. eqlam kirâm u mimma ša abūša iddinušim is “the field, the orchard and whatever her father gave her”: the two accusative objects (A.ŠÀ; {giš}KIRI₆), mimma “whatever”, and ša abūša iddinušim “which her father gave her” (the ša-clause with -šim, as at the start of §178). adi balṭat ikkal is “as long as she is alive she shall eat (have the use of it)”: adi “as long as”, balṭat “she is alive” (stative of balāṭum), ikkal the present of akālum “to eat”, here spelled ì-kal (the sign NI read ì, then KAL); “eat” for “have the use of” is as at §170–177 and UNCERTAIN. ana kaspim ul inaddin is “for silver she shall not give”: kaspim is the Sumerogram KÙ.BABBAR with no ending written.

sentences.l: to-another not she-shall-pay(?); her-heirship of-her-brothers only.
sentences.i: nor shall she use them to pay another (?); her heirs are her brothers alone.
sentences.n: šaniam ul uppal is “to another she shall not pay (?)”: šaniam “another” (accusative or dative of šanûm) and uppal, a present I take to be from apālum “to answer, to pay” (u-up-pa-al); the sense “she may not settle a debt with it either” is UNCERTAIN. ablūssa ša aḫḫīšama is “her heirship belongs to her brothers alone”: ablūssa is ablūtum “the status of an heir” + -ša (t+š written ss, as in warkassa; ab-lu-za), and ša aḫḫīšama is “that of her brothers only” (aḫḫīša is aḫḫū in the genitive, -ma “only”). When she dies, the land passes to her brothers.

sentences.l: If a-priestess(?), a-SAL(?), or-else a-woman a-zikrum, whom her-father a-dowry has-given-her,
sentences.i: If a priestess (?), a SAL-woman (?), or a woman of the zikrum class, to whom her father has given a dowry,
sentences.n: §179 opens exactly as §178 (see there for NIN.AN, SAL, zikrum and the ša-clause); the two laws differ only in what the tablet says. Harper prints zinništi here, the genitive, but SAL shows no ending and as the subject I say zinništum. Harper prints no raised b before the SAL at the end of the first line here; on the plate the sign stands on the same line as NIN.AN.

sentences.l: a-sealed-tablet he-has-written-for-her, in-the-tablet which he-wrote-for-her
sentences.i: and has written a sealed tablet for her, and in the tablet he wrote for her
sentences.n: kunukkam išṭurušim is “a sealed tablet he has written for her”: kunukkum is the tablet closed with the seal (Harper ku-nu-kam, the last sign KAM, as at §153–169); §178 had ṭuppam, the plain tablet. ina ṭuppim ša išṭurušim as before.

sentences.l: her-estate wherever it-is-pleasing to-her to-give he-has-written-for-her-and, as-much-as her-heart he-has-let-her-have,
sentences.i: has written for her that she may give her estate to whomever it pleases her, and has let her have as much as she wishes,
sentences.n: The tablet now says what the tablet of §178 left out: there is no lā before išṭuršimma, and uštamziši (uš-tam-zi-ši, the sign USH read uš) is the perfect where §178 had the preterite ušamziši; the verb is UNCERTAIN as there. The rest is the same wording: warkassa ēma elīša ṭābu nadānam “her estate, to whomever it pleases her, to give”, mala libbiša “as much as her heart (wants)”.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, her-estate wherever it-is-pleasing to-her she-shall-give.
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, she shall give her estate to whomever it pleases her.
sentences.n: The ruling: the estate is hers to give. warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku “after the father has gone to his fate”; warkassa ēma elīša ṭābu inaddin “her estate, wherever it pleases her, she shall give”: inaddin is the present, “she shall give”, the clause the tablet itself contained, now as the law’s own ruling.

sentences.l: her-brothers not shall-claim-against-her.
sentences.i: Her brothers shall not make any claim against her.
sentences.n: aḫḫūša ul ibaqqarūši is “her brothers shall not claim against her”: ibaqqarūši is the present plural of baqārum “to claim” + -ši “her”, as at §141–152, where it is spelled i-ba-qa₂-ru-ši; here Harper’s i-ba-ag-ga-ru-ši has the double q, written AK (read aq) + GA (qa₂). Harper prints the word at line 41 aḫ-hu-ša with a plain h; the plate has the same ḪU sign as in aḫ-ḫu-ša elsewhere, so I write aḫ-ḫu-ša.

sentences.l: If a-father to-his-daughter, a-kallatum(?) or-else a-woman a-zikrum, a-dowry not has-given-her,
sentences.i: If a father has not given a dowry to his daughter, a kallatum (?) or a zikrum-woman,
sentences.n: A new case: the father gave no dowry at all. ana mārtišu is “to his daughter”: DUMU.SAL (two signs) + šu; Harper writes mârti-šu. kallātim is {šal}É.GI₄.A, the woman-sign SAL (Harper’s raised šal, silent here) and the three signs É.GI₄.A, which at §153–169 meant “bride, daughter-in-law”; here it seems to name a class of woman dedicated to a god, which I cannot define: UNCERTAIN. ù lū zinništim zikrum is “or else a woman, a zikrum” as at §178; Harper’s genitive zinništi is zinništim here, since it stands beside mārtišu kallātim in apposition (“his daughter, a kallatum or a zikrum-woman”). šeriqtam lā išruqšim is “a dowry he has not given her”: išruqšim is išruq + -šim, with no -u because this is a plain verb, no ša-clause; the plate shows no sign at the bracketed RU (Harper’s iš-[ru]-uq-ši-im), so the form rests on the same word at §181, iš-ru-uq-ši-im.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, from-the-property of-the-father’s-house a-share like an-heir one she-shall-stand-and,
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, she shall take a share from the property of her father’s house like one heir, and
sentences.n: The ruling: with no dowry, she counts as one more heir. ina makkūr bīt abim is “from the property of her father’s house”: ŠA.GA (makkūr, as at §170), É “house” and a-ba (abim, “of the father”, as at §158). zittam kīma aplim ištēn is “a share like one heir”: zittam is Harper’s ṣi-it-tam (the same word as zi-it-ti-ša, as at §137), aplim “of an heir” (ab-lim), ištēn “one”. izzazma is “she shall stand, and”: izuzzum “to stand”; “stand” with a share is “take her place with it”, my sense, UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: as-long-as she-lives she-shall-have-the-use-of-it; her-estate of-her-brothers only.
sentences.i: she shall have the use of it as long as she lives; after her, her estate belongs to her brothers alone.
sentences.n: adi balṭat ikkal is “as long as she lives she shall have the use of it” (as at §178; here ikkal is spelled out i-ik-ka-al, four signs, where §178 had ì-kal). warkassa ša aḫḫīšama is “her estate belongs to her brothers alone”: warkassa as in §178 (her estate, what she leaves behind; UNCERTAIN where it could also be “her case”, as at §171), ša aḫḫīšama “that of her brothers only”.

sentences.l: If a-father a-qadištum or-else a-NU.PAR to-a-god has-offered-up-and, a-dowry not has-given-her,
sentences.i: If a father has dedicated a qadištum or a NU.PAR to a god, and has not given her a dowry,
sentences.n: Two more classes of dedicated woman. qadištam is {šal}NU.GIG: SAL (Harper’s raised šal, with his own question mark, and it is plainly on the plate) + NU + GIG, the signs for qadištum, “consecrated woman” (Harper qadištu); the exact status of a qadištum is not settled (first time in this work). NU.PAR is the two signs NU and PAR (the sign BAR), a second class of dedicated woman; I give the signs only, with no reading and no translation: UNCERTAIN. ana ilim iššīma is “to a god he has lifted (her), and”: ilim is the single sign AN (DINGIR), and iššīma the preterite of našûm “to lift, bring” + -ma; “dedicated” for “lifted up to a god” is my sense, UNCERTAIN. šeriqtam lā išruqšim as at §180.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, from-the-property of-the-father’s-house a-third of-her-heirship she-shall-stand-and, as-long-as she-lives she-shall-have-the-use-of-it,
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, she shall take one third of her heir’s share from the property of her father’s house, and have the use of it as long as she lives;
sentences.n: As at §180, but the share is one third. IGI.3.GAL is the Sumerogram for “one third”, three signs (IGI, the numeral 3, GAL; Harper’s IGI.III.GAL), said šalšum; before a following noun I give it as šalšat, a reconstruction, marked (?) in the gloss. ablūtiša is “her heirship”: ablūtum (Harper ablûtu, “sonship”, the status of an heir) + -ša, spelled ab-lu-ti-ša; “one third of her heirship” is a third of the share she would have had as an heir. izzazma and adi balṭat ikkal as at §180.

sentences.l: her-estate of-her-brothers only.
sentences.i: her estate belongs to her brothers alone.
sentences.n: warkassa ša aḫḫīšama as at §180: after her death her estate goes to her brothers alone.

sentences.l: If a-father to-his-daughter, a-wife-of Marduk who of-Babylon, a-dowry not has-given-her, a-sealed-tablet not has-written-for-her,
sentences.i: If a father has not given a dowry to his daughter, a wife of Marduk of Babylon, and has not written a sealed tablet for her,
sentences.n: The next class is named after her god. aššat Marduk is “the wife of Marduk”: SAL stands bare and is read aššat (the construct, “wife of”, as at §127–140, where aššatum is written out), and {d}AMAR.UTU is Marduk (the AN sign silent, AMAR.UTU “calf of the sun”, as in the prologue). ša Bābilim is “of Babylon”: the Sumerogram KÁ.DINGIR.RA{ki}, “gate of the god”, read Bābilim (as in the litany), with the KI sign printed full size on the plate. The “wife of Marduk” is a title of a priestess of the god; what more she was I cannot say, UNCERTAIN. šeriqtam lā išruqšim is “a dowry he has not given her”; kunukkam lā išṭuršim is “a sealed tablet he has not written for her”, with no -ma at the end of this protasis.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, from-the-property of-the-father’s-house a-third of-her-heirship with her-brothers she-shall-stand-and, the-fief-duty not she-shall-go;
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, she shall take one third of her heir’s share from the property of her father’s house together with her brothers, and she shall not perform the fief-duty;
sentences.n: She takes a third, as at §181, and owes no service on it. itti aḫḫīša izzazma is “with her brothers she shall stand (take her place), and”. ilkam ul illak is “she shall not perform the fief-duty”: ilkam is ilkum written il-kam (the signs IL and KAM, as the “fief-duty” of §26–41), with ul … illak “she shall not go”; alākum “to go” with ilkum is “to carry out the service”. The reason is not stated; I take it that the share she receives is free of the service her brothers’ shares carry, UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: the-wife-of Marduk her-estate wherever it-is-pleasing to-her she-shall-give.
sentences.i: The wife of Marduk shall give her estate to whomever it pleases her.
sentences.n: The last ruling: the estate is hers to give, as at §179. aššat Marduk as above; warkassa ēma elīša ṭābu inaddin as at §179. The unit runs from column XXXI (line 93) into the first line of column XXXII, where inaddin stands alone on its line.

sentences.l: If a-father to-his-daughter, a-šugītum, a-dowry has-given-her, to-a-husband has-given-her, a-sealed-tablet has-written-for-her,
sentences.i: If a father has given a dowry to his daughter, a šugītum, and has given her to a husband, and has written a sealed tablet for her,
sentences.n: The šugītum is the woman first met at §137 (there with a raised SAL; Harper prints šu-ge-tim here without it, and the plate shows only the three signs ŠU, GI₄, TIM). ana mārtišu šugītim is “to his daughter, a šugītum”, in apposition. šeriqtam išruqšim is “a dowry he has given her”, with no lā this time; ana mutim iddišši is “to a husband he has given her”: mutim is “husband” (short u, as at §127–140) and iddišši is iddin + -ši “her”, the n written as š (id-di-iš-ši). kunukkam išṭuršim is “a sealed tablet he has written for her” (ku-nu-uk-kam, the sign UG read uk). This is a protasis; the ruling is the next unit.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone, from-the-property of-the-father’s-house not she-shall-stand.
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate, she shall have no share in the property of her father’s house.
sentences.n: She has already had her dowry and her husband, so she gets no more. ina makkūr bīt abim ul izzaz is “in the property of her father’s house she shall not stand (have a share)”: the same ŠA.GA, É and a-ba as at §180–182, and ul izzaz is izuzzum with ul, the opposite of the izzazma of those laws.

sentences.l: If a-man to-his-daughter, a-šugītum, a-dowry not has-given-her, to-a-husband not has-given-her,
sentences.i: If a man has not given a dowry to his daughter, a šugītum, and has not given her to a husband,
sentences.n: The opposite case from §183: neither dowry nor husband. This law says awīlum “a man” where the others had abum “a father”. Both verbs have lā: šeriqtam lā išruqšim “a dowry he has not given her” (Harper’s iš-ru-uq-šim, with the single sign TAG read šim) and ana mutim lā iddišši “to a husband he has not given her”.

sentences.l: after the-father to-fate has-gone,
sentences.i: After the father has gone to his fate,
sentences.n: warka abum ana šīmtim ittalku, the same clause as in every law of this part (§170: “after the father has gone to his fate”); the ruling follows.

sentences.l: her-brothers in-proportion-to the-strength of-the-father’s-house a-dowry shall-give-her-and to-a-husband shall-give-her.
sentences.i: her brothers shall give her a dowry in proportion to the means of her father’s house, and shall give her to a husband.
sentences.n: The ruling: the brothers must provide for her. aḫḫūša kīma emūq bīt abim is “her brothers, in proportion to the strength of her father’s house” (emūq “strength”, as at §178; “means” is my English for it): kīma + emūq + bīt abim, with É and a-ba. šeriqtam išarraqūšima is “they shall give her a dowry, and”: išarraqū is the present plural of šarāqum (the same verb as išruq above, with its middle r doubled), then -ši “her” and -ma, spelled i-šar-ra-qu₂-ši-ma. ana mutim inaddinūši is “to a husband they shall give her”: inaddinū the present plural of nadānum + -ši.
